abstract.p: Nanopolysaccharides (NPSs) constitute a rapidly advancing class of biodegradable and biocompatible nanomaterials with strong potential to support sustainable, climate-resilient agriculture. NPSs exhibit high surface area, tunable surface chemistry, and enhanced interactions with biological interfaces, enabling multifunctional roles across soil–plant–microbe systems. This review provides a function-guided synthesis of recent advances in NPS-based agricultural applications, structured around ten interconnected functional domains. These include: (i) structural classes of NPSs and their surface-chemistry-driven functionality; (ii) soil improvement and moisture regulation; (iii) slow and controlled release of mineral fertilizers (e.g., NPK, urea, ammonium and phosphate salts); (iv) foliar delivery for nutrient uptake and stress mitigation; (v) direct antibacterial and antifungal activity against major phytopathogens; (vi) antiviral strategies, including nano-enabled RNA interference delivery; (vii) nano-loading and targeted delivery of agrochemicals, micronutrients, and botanical actives; (viii) induction of plant defense and immune priming; and (ix) encapsulation and nanocoating of agriculturally important microbial inoculants to enhance survival, controlled release, and field performance; and (x) seed nanopriming for improved germination, stress resilience, and early vigor. Emphasis is placed on structure–function relationships linking nanoparticle size, surface charge, crystallinity, functional group density, and cross-linking chemistry to agronomic outcomes, providing a framework for rational design of next-generation NPS-based agricultural formulations.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The emergence of nanopolysaccharides (NPSs) as a novel group of nanomaterials has opened up new opportunities in various areas, including agriculture [1–7]. In the era of global climate change, the main challenges in agriculture include mitigating abiotic and biotic stresses on plants; developing antimicrobial agents to protect plants from phytopathogenic viruses, bacteria, and fungi; designing effective agrochemicals for seed treatment; enhancing plant growth and development under stress conditions; optimizing mineral fertilizer application rates; and developing efficient encapsulation and coating agents for beneficial microbes. In this respect, NPSs have proven to be promising and environmentally friendly candidates [8–11]. NPSs are particularly important for their high biocompatibility, biodegradability, and enhanced mechanical properties [12, 13]. They also offer eco-friendly solutions in biomedicine, sustainability, and materials science [12].

NPSs are nanoscale derivatives of PSs with enhanced properties like increased surface area, reactivity, and bioavailability. They are biodegradable, derived from renewable resources, and synthesized through various methods [6]. NPSs enhance agrochemical delivery, improve soil fertility, promote plant growth, and reduce environmental impact [6, 7, 14]. NPSs are reported to enhance the biological functions of agriculturally important microbial strains [8–11].

Although several recent reviews have discussed NPSs in agriculture, often focusing on specific polymer classes, selected application domains, or general nano-enabled crop protection concepts [1–7, 15], they typically provide application summaries rather than a comparative, performance-guided evaluation across multiple agricultural functions. In contrast, the present review consolidates advances in NPS types, and their multifunctional roles across the soil–plant–microbe system. Specifically, it integrates ten interconnected functional domains within a single framework: (i) structural classes of NPSs and their surface-chemistry-driven functionality; (ii) soil improvement and moisture regulation; (iii) slow and controlled release of mineral fertilizers (e.g., NPK, urea, ammonium and phosphate salts); (iv) foliar delivery for nutrient uptake and stress mitigation; (v) direct antibacterial and antifungal activity against major phytopathogens; (vi) antiviral strategies, including nano-enabled RNA interference delivery; (vii) nano-loading and targeted delivery of agrochemicals, micronutrients, and botanical actives; (viii) induction of plant defense and immune priming; and (ix) encapsulation and nanocoating of agriculturally important microbial inoculants to enhance survival, controlled release, and field performance, (x) seed nanopriming for improved germination, stress resilience, and early vigor. Therefore, this review provides an evidence-based comparison to identify the most suitable NPSs platforms for specific agricultural purposes based on performance, feasibility, and biosafety.

The functional superiority of NPSs over their bulk counterparts arises from fundamental changes in macromolecular organization imposed by nanoscale confinement. Reduction of PS assemblies to the nanometer scale restricts polymer chain mobility, increases surface-to-volume ratio, and exposes a high density of reactive functional groups, thereby amplifying intermolecular interactions with biological interfaces [12–14, 16]. Parameters such as polymer chain length, crystallinity, surface charge, degree of acetylation or substitution, and cross-linking density collectively determine nanoparticle stability, hydration behavior, and affinity toward plant tissues and microbial cells [17, 18].

In contrast to bulk PSs, NPSs operate as surface-dominated macromolecular systems, where electrostatic interactions, hydrogen bonding, and steric effects govern biological activity rather than bulk material properties [19, 20]. Consequently, nanoscale morphology and chemical functionality directly regulate antimicrobial efficacy, nutrient binding, controlled release behavior, and defense signaling in plants, providing a unifying macromolecular framework for understanding their diverse agricultural applications [21–25].

Studies involving NPSs have been conducted in a range of crop species, including wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) [26, 27], maize (Zea mays L.) [28–33], tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) [34–36], wild blueberry (Vaccinium myrtilloides) and lowbush blueberry (Vaccinium angustifolium) [37], French bean [38], pearl and finger millets [22, 23, 39], balangu (Lallemantia iberica) [40], strawberry [41–43], pepper [20], tobacco (Nicotiana glutinosa) [44], chickpea [45], rice (Oryza sativa L.) [46, 47], soybean (Glycine max (L.)) [48], and melon [49].

sec.title: Review methodology
sec.p: This review was prepared through a structured literature search and screening process focused on nanopolysaccharide-based nanoformulations and their multifunctional roles in sustainable agriculture. Peer-reviewed publications were identified using major scientific databases including Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and Google Scholar. The search strategy combined keywords related to polysaccharide nanomaterials with agricultural applications, using terms such as: nanopolysaccharide, nanochitosan, nanocellulose, cellulose nanocrystal (CNC), cellulose nanofibril (CNF), bacterial nanocellulose, alginate nanoparticles, starch nanoparticles, pectin nanoparticles, dextran nanoparticles, pullulan nanoparticles, in combination with agriculture-oriented terms including soil improvement, controlled release fertilizer, slow release NPK, urea release, nutrient-use efficiency, foliar fertilization, antifungal, antibacterial, phytopathogens, antiviral, TMV, AMV, RNA interference, siRNA/dsRNA delivery, agrochemical delivery, pesticide encapsulation, herbicide, fungicide, and plant immunity/defense priming.

The initial search results were screened by title and abstract to remove duplicates and non-relevant records. Eligible studies were then evaluated by full-text assessment using predefined inclusion criteria. The review prioritized (i) studies reporting NPSs derived from renewable polysaccharides (cellulose, chitosan, alginate, starch, pectin, dextran, pullulan, etc.); (ii) studies providing experimental evidence of agricultural relevance including soil conditioning, mineral nutrient delivery, foliar application, antimicrobial/antiviral performance, agrochemical loading, or induction of plant defense responses; and (iii) studies presenting measurable outcomes such as nanoparticle size and morphology, encapsulation efficiency, release kinetics, pathogen inhibition, plant physiological indices (growth, yield, nutrient uptake), or defense markers (PR proteins, PAL/PO/PPO, antioxidant enzymes, WRKY, phenolics).

Exclusion criteria included articles unrelated to plant/soil systems (pure biomedical-only studies without agricultural relevance), reports lacking experimental validation, or papers focusing solely on bulk polysaccharides without nanoscale formulation. Priority was given to recent publications (primarily 2018–2026) to capture current progress in nano-enabled agriculture, while highly cited foundational papers were retained to support key mechanistic concepts and material characterization principles.

After selection, the included studies were synthesized into a performance-guided comparative framework covering ten interconnected functional domains: (1) structural classes of NPSs and their functional relevance; (2) soil improvement and controlled/slow-release fertilization; (3) foliar application and stress mitigation; (4) antibacterial and antifungal activity; (5) antiviral strategies including RNAi-oriented delivery concepts; (6) nano-enabled loading and targeted delivery of agrochemicals and bioactive inputs; (7) induction of plant defense and immune priming; (8) encapsulation and nanocoating of beneficial microbial inoculants; (9) seed nanopriming; and (10) emerging future applications including biodegradable composite systems and hydroponic platforms. The review emphasizes structure–function relationships, where nanoparticle size, surface charge, crystallinity, degree of acetylation/substitution, and cross-linking chemistry were interpreted as key determinants of stability, release behavior, microbial interaction, and plant response.

sec.title: Structural classes of NPSs and their functional relevance in agriculture
sec.p: Nanopolysaccharide nanomaterials include cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs), cellulose nanofibrils (CNFs), bacterial nanocellulose (BNC), regenerated nanocellulose (RNC), chitosan nanoparticles, often referred to as nanochitosan (CSNPs), alginate nanoparticles (AlgNPs), starch nanoparticles (SNPs), pectin nanoparticles (PNPs), dextran nanoparticles (DNPs), pullulan nanoparticles (PLNPs), and hyaluronic acid nanoparticles (HANPs).

The agricultural performance of NPSs is primarily dictated by their dominant surface chemistry and nanoscale interactions, rather than their biological origin. –OH–rich nanocellulose (NC) systems form highly hydrated, hydrogen-bonded networks that enhance soil aggregation, water retention, and diffusion-controlled nutrient release, making them particularly effective for soil improvement and slow/controlled-release fertilizer applications [50–52]. In contrast, –NH₂–rich CSNPs exhibits strong cationic interactions with microbial cells and plant tissues, resulting in broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity and effective induction of plant defense responses, thereby supporting sustainable plant disease management [53, 54]. Ionotropically crosslinked alginate NPs, typically formed via Ca²⁺-mediated gelation, enable tunable encapsulation and controlled release of agrochemicals and bioactive compounds, serving as versatile nano-delivery platforms for crop protection and weed management [55–58]. Alginate is a linear anionic polysaccharide composed of β-D-mannuronic acid and α-L-guluronic acid residues containing abundant carboxylate (–COO⁻) groups, which are responsible for its unique ion-binding properties [55–58]. These negatively charged functional groups readily chelate divalent cations, particularly Ca²⁺, forming the characteristic “egg-box” hydrogel network that provides excellent encapsulation capacity and tunable controlled-release behavior for fertilizers and other agricultural compounds [55–58]. Similar carboxylate-rich polysaccharides, such as pectin, also form ionically crosslinked hydrogel matrices that contribute to encapsulation efficiency and sustained release of bioactive agents [15, 58].

In summary, the agricultural performance of nanopolysaccharides is governed by their dominant surface functional groups, hydroxyl (–OH), amino (–NH₂), and carboxylate (–COO⁻). Precise control of these groups enables targeted functions in soil structuring and water retention, controlled nutrient release, and plant protection, positioning NPSs as adaptable tools for sustainable agriculture.

sec.title: NPSs for soil improvement and controlled nutrient delivery
sec.p: NPSs are increasingly applied for soil improvement due to their ability to enhance soil structure, moisture conservation, and nutrient availability [6, 7, 59]. In particular, these NPSs support nutrient-use efficiency by improving nutrient retention in soils, reducing losses, and enabling more efficient delivery of mineral elements to plants, as summarized in Table 1 [7, 60]. Owing to their nanoscale dimensions and large specific surface area, NPSs carriers can interact strongly with soil particles, promoting aggregation, increasing porosity, limiting erosion, and improving the physical environment for root development. Collectively, these properties translate into improved plant performance and productivity while supporting more sustainable soil fertility management.

sec.p: The controlled-release performance of different nanopolysaccharides originates from their distinct structural and physicochemical characteristics rather than from nanoscale dimensions alone [12, 13, 17, 18]. NC possesses a crystalline fibrillar or nanoparticulate architecture enriched with surface hydroxyl groups, which promotes hydration and the formation of interconnected hydrogen-bonded networks [12, 13, 50–52]. These hydrated networks retain water and create tortuous diffusion pathways that restrict the rapid migration of dissolved nutrients, thereby supporting their gradual release from nanocellulose-based fertilizer matrices [24, 25, 51, 52]. CSNPs contain protonatable amino groups whose charge state depends on the surrounding pH, allowing electrostatic association with anionic nutrient species and other negatively charged compounds [17–19, 54]. During ionic or covalent crosslinking, chitosan chains form compact three-dimensional matrices that physically entrap nutrients and reduce their diffusion into the external medium [18, 47, 54]. In contrast, alginate-based nanoparticles and hydrogels are formed mainly through ionotropic crosslinking of carboxylate-rich alginate chains with divalent cations, particularly Ca²⁺, producing the characteristic “egg-box” network [55–57]. Variation in crosslinking density, network porosity, hydration, and swelling consequently regulates the diffusion and release of encapsulated agrochemicals or bioactive compounds from alginate matrices [55–58]. Therefore, nutrient-release kinetics from NPS carriers are collectively governed by polymer crystallinity, surface functional groups, electrostatic interactions, crosslinking density, matrix porosity, hydration capacity, swelling behaviour, and gradual polymer degradation [24, 25, 51, 52, 54–58].

Among the NPSs, CSNPs has been widely reported as a multifunctional soil-enhancing material that promotes soil structure stabilization, nutrient availability, and organic matter accumulation [5, 69]. CSNPs-based fertilizer systems have demonstrated clear agronomic benefits, including improved wheat growth and yield in sandy soils when formulated as CSNPs–NPK [61]. Similarly, potassium-loaded CSNPs significantly increased strawberry productivity and fruit quality parameters, including vitamin C, total sugars, and anthocyanins [42]. Consistently, CSNPs application under sandy soil conditions enhanced wheat growth performance alongside increased nutrient availability [27]. Because fabrication strategies vary considerably among different nanopolysaccharide classes, no single preparation method is universally applicable. Other NPSs, including NC, AlgNPs, SNPs, and DNPs, are produced through different fabrication approaches depending on their polymer chemistry and intended agricultural application.

sec.p: Nanocellulose-based materials, including CNC and CNF, represent the most extensively documented NPSs platforms in agriculture [7, 24, 59, 62, 70, 71]. CNF is particularly effective for soil conditioning due to its water-absorbing behavior and soil-binding capacity, which improves aggregate stability, promotes macro-aggregate formation, and enhances soil water retention. Notably, incorporation of 1% CNF increased soil water content by 98% and extended water retention by 22 days, highlighting its relevance for drought-prone environments [50]. Functionalized NC systems further support nutrient management: carboxylated NC and CNC were reported to improve soil moisture retention and urea efficiency, and when combined with hydroxyapatite, increased fresh and dry biomass by 32% and 26%, respectively, in sandy loam soil [70]. Moreover, NC composites formulated with starch and black tea extract have been shown to exert beneficial effects on soil health [72].

Beyond soil conditioning, NC modulates nitrogen transformation pathways. Dai et al. (2022) showed that nanocellulose applied during composting (300–900 mg kg⁻¹) maximized nitrogen retention at 900 mg kg⁻¹ by reducing ammonia emissions, enhancing ammonium oxidation (increased amoA), and lowering nirK abundance, with implications for N₂O formation [73]. At this dose, nanocellulose also increased Rhizobiales abundance, indicating enhanced nitrogen fixation potential [73].

A major strength of NC lies in its repeated documentation as a biodegradable matrix for the slow and controlled release of mineral fertilizers. CNFs-encapsulated potassium nitrate (KNO₃), integrated into a biodegradable matrix, enabled nutrient release over 8 h in water and up to 80 days in soil, while achieving 75% biodegradation within 120 days [25]. Modified CNF has also been used to encapsulate (NH₄)₂HPO₄, ensuring controlled diffusion of NH₄⁺ and PO₄³⁻ ions [63]. Hybrid systems combining cellulose nanofibers with engineered biochar have further been developed as biodegradable coatings for slow-release phosphate fertilizers [66]. In urea delivery, CNF was incorporated into urea-loaded hydrogel formulations achieving 92% urea loading (w/w) with substantial water absorption capacity (147 g/g) [64]. Similarly, rice straw-derived CNF loaded with ammonium chloride released 58% of ammonium ions over 8 days [65].

Consistent with these findings, CNFs have been repeatedly validated for slow/controlled mineral fertilizer delivery [67, 68]. Encapsulation strategies targeting nitrogen- and potassium-based nutrients were shown to regulate release kinetics and support enhanced-efficiency fertilizer concepts [67], while nitrogen-loaded CNFs formulations also supported microbial growth under soil burial conditions, emphasizing their compatibility with soil microbial ecosystems [68]. NC has additionally been incorporated into fertilizer-strengthening composites; for example, a biodegradable CNC–PVA nanocomposite extended NPK nutrient release to 10–30 days while improving soil water retention, with crushing strength optimized at 14.5 wt% CNC [62]. Importantly, NC-based systems also mitigate nutrient losses through leaching. NC and Zn-modified NC combined with NPK significantly reduced nitrogen leaching, addressing a key limitation of micronutrient and macronutrient fertilization strategies [60]. Accordingly, CNFs-based platforms continue to emerge as promising sustainable nanobiomaterials for soil improvement and nutrient efficiency [70, 74].

Overall, NPSs are biodegradable platforms that enhance soil quality and enable slow/controlled fertilizer release, improving nutrient-use efficiency. Nanocellulose (CNC/CNF) is the most consistently reported carrier for regulated delivery of mineral nutrients (e.g., NPK, urea, KNO₃, ammonium/phosphate salts), while CSNPs is also well documented for coating and encapsulation. Their highlighted properties support controlled nutrient diffusion, better rhizosphere performance, and reduced fertilizer losses.

sec.title: Foliar application of NPSs
sec.p: Beyond soil-based delivery systems, NPSs can also be applied directly to crops through foliar spraying to enhance germination, nutrient uptake, and stress tolerance [75–77]. The reduction in water resources and drastic changes in soil and climatic conditions have necessitated a serious reconsideration of fertilization strategies [77]. In this context, foliar fertilization is increasingly adopted as an efficient approach in modern agriculture [77]. Beyond conventional agrochemicals, NPSs are gaining prominence as foliar-applied materials for improving plant performance [37–39, 78]. Foliar NPSs can enhance leaf-surface wettability and reduce water loss by modifying spray–leaf interactions [37]. In addition, they promote mineral uptake and may be translocated via the phloem from leaves to roots, showing stronger performance in clay–sandy soils than in clay soils [78]. Foliar NPS application can also stimulate defense-related enzymes, including chitinase, β-1,3-glucanase, chitosanase, protease inhibitors, peroxidase, and polyphenol oxidase, thereby strengthening plant immunity [39]. Moreover, foliar NPSs have been reported to mitigate metal stress [34] and enhance drought tolerance [28]. For example, in melon, foliar application of CSNPs improved fruit yield and nutraceutical quality in a dose-dependent manner, with 0.4 mg mL⁻¹ maximizing productivity, whereas 0.8 mg mL⁻¹ enhanced postharvest traits, antioxidant capacity, and bioactive compound accumulation [49].

Tasnim et al. (2023) reported that CNFs modified leaf–spray interactions in wild lowbush blueberries by improving surface wettability and reducing water loss in Vaccinium myrtilloides, while enhancing foliar fertilizer dispersion into finer particles on V. angustifolium leaves, which may contribute to increased fruit yield [37]. Abdel-Aziz et al. (2018) found that foliar application of a CSNPs-based NPK fertilizer in wheat shortened the crop life cycle by 23.5% (≈ 130 days to yield) and significantly improved yield traits compared with conventional and non-fertilized controls [78]. Similarly, Hasaneen et al. (2016) demonstrated that carbon nanotube–coated NPK and CSNPs–NPK nanofertilizers significantly enhanced French bean growth and biomass within ~ 30 days compared with the control [38].

Sathiyabama and Manikandan (2021) showed that CSNPs applied as a foliar treatment improved finger millet growth, yield, and mineral uptake (Fe, Zn, Mn, P, Ca, and Mg) more effectively than bulk chitosan and controls, while simultaneously inducing defense enzymes [39]. In tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), foliar application of CSNPs(100 µg/mL) alleviated Cd stress by increasing shoot dry weight (+ 38%), photosynthesis (+ 45%), and SPAD index (+ 40%), while reducing oxidative stress markers (MDA − 24% and H₂O₂ −20%) [34]. Under water deficit, CSNPs combined with Myco-Root enhanced balangu (Lallemantia iberica) growth, photosynthesis, antioxidant activity, and essential oil yield and quality [40]. Under drought stress, Rukhsar et al. (2026) reported that foliar-applied CSNPs improved drought tolerance in Zea mays L. in a dose-dependent manner, with 50 mg L⁻¹ producing the strongest response by increasing shoot biomass (+ 28%), root length (+ 22%), chlorophyll content (+ 35%), antioxidant enzyme activities (up to + 45%), K⁺ uptake (+ 18%), and soluble protein content (+ 30%) compared with untreated drought-stressed plants [28].

Collectively, NPSs-based foliar fertilization offers an effective, climate-smart strategy to improve spray efficiency, nutrient uptake, and stress tolerance, thereby sustaining yield under drought and metal stress. Further optimization of formulation, dosage, and long-term field safety is still needed.

sec.title: NPSs as antibacterial and antifungal agents in agriculture
sec.p: NPSs generally exhibit stronger antimicrobial activity than their bulk PS counterparts, primarily due to their higher specific surface area, enhanced cellular interaction/uptake, and increased surface charge density [79–81]. The antimicrobial performance of NPSs is governed not only by nanoscale dimensions but also by their surface chemistry and interaction mechanisms with microbial cells. Among the different NPSs, CSNPs exhibit the strongest intrinsic antimicrobial activity because protonated amino groups (–NH₃⁺) electrostatically interact with negatively charged components of fungal and bacterial cell envelopes, promoting membrane destabilization, increased permeability, leakage of intracellular constituents, and ultimately growth inhibition [17, 21, 79–81]. These membrane perturbations are frequently accompanied by oxidative stress and excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, further contributing to cellular damage and pathogen suppression [17, 21, 79]. In contrast, NC generally exhibits limited intrinsic antimicrobial activity but provides an excellent high-surface-area platform for immobilizing antimicrobial compounds or metallic nanoparticles, thereby enhancing their stability, dispersion, and sustained antimicrobial efficacy [20, 82–86]. Indeed, the nanoscale size difference is considered a major factor underlying the superior bioactivity of NPSs relative to bulk PSs [45]. In agriculture, antimicrobial effects have been most consistently demonstrated for CSNPs and, to a lesser extent, CNC, which have been widely tested as antibacterial/antifungal agents (Table 2) [1, 15, 17, 79, 80, 82, 87]. A representative comparative study by Saharan et al. (2013) showed that CSNPs inhibited Alternaria alternata, Macrophomina phaseolina, and Rhizoctonia solani by 82%, 88%, and 34%, respectively, whereas bulk chitosan achieved only 21%, 18%, and 17% inhibition, highlighting the potency gain achieved through nanosizing [88].

sec.p: Across studies, CSNPs displays broad-spectrum antifungal activity, suppressing major phytopathogens including Fusarium oxysporum, Alternaria solani, and Pyricularia grisea [87], Fusarium graminearum [79], Botrytis cinerea [41, 43], and A. alternata, Verticillium dahliae, and Bipolaris sorokiniana [88, 92]. Additional reports document inhibitory effects against Aspergillus flavus [76], Harpophora maydis [81], and Colletotrichum species (Colletotrichum musae and Colletotrichum chrysophillum) [93]. In the latter study, CSNPs (302.4 ± 92.3 nm) reduced radial growth of C. chrysophillum by 21%, while C. musae showed maximal inhibition (26%) at 1.5 mg/mL [93]. In parallel, nanocellulose materials have also been examined as antimicrobial agents: CNC inhibited Colletotrichum gloeosporioides [82], while nanocellulose-based systems suppressed R. solani (Kuhn) [46]. Moreover, CNCs derived from agricultural waste (e.g., hazelnut pruning residues) demonstrated notable in vitro and in vivo antibacterial activity against plant pathogens, supporting a sustainable crop-protection approach [83].

Beyond standalone NPSs, antimicrobial potency is frequently enhanced through functionalization and composite formation, enabling stronger activity and broader pathogen control [20, 84]. For example, encapsulation of Nepeta hormozganica and Nepeta dschuprensis essential oils within CSNPs increased antifungal efficiency up to 100% against six phytopathogenic fungi, including F. oxysporum, (A) alternata, and (B) cinerea [84]. Similarly, a bio-based nano-antifungal system produced by coating CNC with hexadecyl trimethyl ammonium bromide (CTAB) achieved 100% antifungal activity against Phytophthora capsici [20]. Metal-associated CSNPs systems represent another effective class; Cu–CSNPs inhibited Curvularia lunata, significantly suppressing mycelial growth under in vitro conditions [32]. Choudhary et al. (2017) further evaluated Cu–chitosan nanocomposites against Fusarium verticillioides, reinforcing the antimicrobial relevance of Cu-functionalized chitosan systems [31].

Recent studies increasingly report antimicrobial NPSs composites based on NC or chitosan matrices coupled with inorganic nanoparticles or active ingredients. Santos et al. (2024) developed antifungal bionanocomposites composed of silver nanoparticles (AgNPSs), NFC derived from eucalyptus, and cassava starch, which inhibited Botrytis cinerea, Penicillium expansum, C. musae, and Fusarium semitectum [85]. Likewise, a NC–TiO₂ nanobiocomposite showed strong biocidal activity against Phytophthora spp. at 0.125 mg/mL and F. graminearum at 0.25 mg/mL [86]. Essential-oil nanoencapsulation strategies have also proven effective; a formulation based on carboxylated NC and lemongrass essential oil exhibited superior inhibition of A. flavus mycelial growth [94]. In another example, CSNPs loaded with Thymus vulgaris essential oil exerted strong antifungal activity against F. solani affecting Solanum lycopersicum, with marked suppression of radial mycelial growth at 1.0% concentration [95].

Nanoformulations have additionally been developed as pesticide delivery platforms with enhanced antifungal performance. Kumar et al. (2022) reported mancozeb-loaded chitosan–carrageenan nanocomposites (66.6–231.82 nm) that inhibited A. alternata, A. solani, Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, and Stemphylium lycopersici, achieving 100% inhibition of S. lycopersici and S. sclerotiorum at 1.0 and 1.5 ppm, respectively, comparable to commercial mancozeb [96]. In contrast, inhibition of A. solani was lower (67.7 ± 1.4% at 0.5 ppm; 67.7 ± 0% at 1.0 ppm) but improved to 83.1 ± 0% at 1.5 ppm, approaching commercial efficacy (84.6 ± 0%). Blank nanoparticles exhibited minimal inhibition (50 ± 3.5%, fungal growth 32.5 ± 3.5 mm), and the nanocomposites were overall most effective against S. sclerotiorum, followed by S. lycopersici and A. alternata [96]. Beyond direct inhibition, CSNPs can also support host resistance; Siddaiah et al. (2018) reported that CSNPs with a high degree of acetylation enhanced resistance against pearl millet downy mildew caused by the biotrophic oomycete Sclerospora graminicola [22].

NC has further demonstrated value as an antimicrobial nanocarrier within nanostructured pesticide systems. Schiavi et al. (2021) reported significant antibacterial activity against Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato using a nanostructured pesticide composed of chitosan hydrochloride as the active ingredient, CNC as the nanocarrier, and starch as an excipient; notably, this system displayed ~ 50% loading capacity and sustained release over 24 h [91]. Similarly, a novel composite biopolymer system Cls-Alg@ZnO [36]. ZnO nanoparticles integrated with cellulose and alginate) was evaluated for tomato growth promotion and immune enhancement against P. syringae pv. tomato and exhibited strong antifungal activity against A. solani, Cladosporium fulvum, F. oxysporum f. sp. lycopersici, F. oxysporum f. sp. dianthi, F. oxysporum f. sp. melonis, Stemphylium sp., and V. dahliae; application of 300 µg mL⁻¹ markedly suppressed F. oxysporum mycelial growth [36].

Overall, NPSs constitute eco-friendly antimicrobial tools for agriculture by providing direct antibacterial and antifungal activity and supporting crop protection against major phytopathogens. Among the reviewed materials, CSNPs is the best-documented and most consistently effective NPSs, exhibiting broad-spectrum activity against diverse fungal genera (Fusarium, Alternaria, Botrytis, Rhizoctonia, Aspergillus, Colletotrichum, etc.) and several bacterial pathogens. In comparison, NC-based systems also contribute to antimicrobial performance; however, they are more frequently reported as nanocarriers within composites or pesticide delivery platforms rather than as strong standalone antimicrobial agents.

sec.title: NPSs as antiviral agents in agriculture
sec.p: Plant viruses pose a significant challenge to sustainable crop production worldwide. Among available antiviral strategies, nanotechnology has emerged as a promising approach for mitigating plant viral diseases. Numerous studies have demonstrated the antiviral activity of NPSs, particularly CSNPs, which can inhibit infection through direct virion disruption and interference with viral replication [97], as summarized in Table 2. The antiviral activity of NPSs also depends on structure-dependent physicochemical interactions. Owing to their cationic surface charge, CSNPs efficiently bind negatively charged nucleic acids through electrostatic interactions, protecting siRNAs and dsRNAs from nuclease-mediated degradation while improving their stability during delivery [14, 90]. Their nanoscale dimensions further facilitate cellular uptake and endocytic internalization into plant tissues, enabling efficient transport of RNA molecules to intracellular sites where RNA interference (RNAi) pathways suppress viral gene expression [90]. In addition, chitosan-based nanoformulations can enhance adhesion to plant surfaces and prolong the residence time of antiviral agents, thereby increasing delivery efficiency and reducing premature loss under field conditions [14, 90]. For instance, CSNPs can encapsulate small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) or double-stranded RNAs (dsRNAs), enabling their delivery into plant cells and activation of RNA interference pathways that degrade viral mRNA, thereby suppressing viral protein synthesis and replication [90]. In addition, CSNPs formulations enhance RNA stability and cellular uptake, overcoming limitations associated with naked RNA application, including rapid degradation and poor penetration [90]. Certain formulations may also form a protective “nano-net” layer on plant surfaces, physically limiting viral attachment and subsequent infection [35].

Khalil et al. (2022) applied CSNPs against Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) and the root-knot nematode Meloidogyne incognita [89]. El-Ganainy et al. (2023) evaluated CSNPs and chitosan–silver nanocomposites (CS–Ag NC) against alfalfa mosaic virus (AMV) in pepper, reporting inhibition rates of 90% and 91% following foliar application of 400 ppm CS-NPSs or 200 ppm CS–Ag NC at 24 h post inoculation [14]. Abdelkhalek et al. (2021) synthesized CSNPs/DNPs (20–160 nm) and demonstrated strong antiviral activity against AMV in Nicotiana glutinosa, accompanied by enhanced innate immune responses [44]. In vitro studies further support that diverse NPSs suppress viral replication and infectivity across a range of plant viruses, providing foundational evidence for their antiviral potential [22].

Beyond direct antiviral effects, nanoformulations may improve agronomic traits (plant height, fresh and dry pod weights, and pod number) [14] and stimulate plant immunity [44]. CSNPs have been shown to upregulate defense-related genes and increase total phenolic content, supporting broad-spectrum resistance responses [98]. Overall, NPSs act as antiviral agents by reducing infection and enhancing host resistance through immune priming. Among the reviewed materials, CSNPs (including CSNPs and chitosan-based nanocomposites) remains the most extensively documented and the most promising antiviral NP, demonstrating strong inhibitory effects against key plant viruses (e.g., TMV and AMV) and promoting plant defense activation.

sec.p: Unlike Sect. 3, which focuses on mineral fertilizers, this section addresses nano-enabled delivery of agrochemicals, including pesticides, herbicides, fungicides, elicitors, and micronutrients. Because these cargoes differ fundamentally from inorganic nutrients in their physicochemical properties, their encapsulation and delivery require different nanopolysaccharide design strategies.

Kumar et al. (2014) encapsulated imidacloprid in sodium alginate nanoparticles (50–100 nm), and the resulting nanoformulation exhibited superior activity against leafhoppers relative to the conventional pesticide [100]. Similarly, Kumar et al. (2015) investigated the fabrication of AlgNPs–CSNPs loaded with acetamiprid; the particles were spherical, with an encapsulation efficiency of 62% [101]. Dos Santos Silva et al. (2011) developed AlgNPs/CSNPs loaded with paraquat (1,1′-dimethyl-4,4′-bipyridyl), a non-selective contact herbicide [99]. AlgNPs/CSNPs have also been used to encapsulate cartap hydrochloride, producing stable nanospheres (107.58–173.07 nm) with an encapsulation efficiency of 76.19% and storage stability of up to 30 days at ambient temperature [102].

Beyond insecticides, herbicides can also be incorporated into nanoparticle systems. Maruyama et al. (2016) encapsulated imazapic and imazapyr in AlgNPs/CSNPs, enhancing efficacy, minimizing toxicity to non-target organisms, and reducing environmental contamination risks [103].

Xiong et al. (2024) developed a dextran-based delivery system for tebuconazole in tomato plants [104]. Spherical nanoparticles were produced via two-step dextran esterification followed by pesticide loading. In vitro antifungal assays and pot experiments showed that the nanoformulation increased tebuconazole inhibition of Botrytis cinerea by 58.4% and improved protection against tomato gray mold by 74.9% compared with commercial suspensions.

Kumar et al. (2022) reported mancozeb-loaded chitosan–carrageenan nanocomposites (66.6–231.82 nm) [96]. In addition, Leonardi et al. (2021) fabricated a nanofertilizer by incorporating CuO nanoparticles into AlgNPs/CSNPs, which improved the germination performance of Fortunella margarita Swingle seeds [107]. Calcium alginate nanocarriers have also been used to load iron (Fe) for controlled release, resulting in enhanced plant growth compared with direct Fe application to soil [108].

SNPs have demonstrated potential for encapsulating botanical fungicides such as carvacrol, enabling sustained release and improved efficacy against pathogens including B. cinerea [105]. Mugo et al. (2024) further reported that bovine biowaste-derived NC effectively stabilized pyrethrins and enabled controlled release for up to one month, showing functional similarity to commercial CNCs [106]. Finally, CSNPs have been used to encapsulate diverse elicitors and micronutrients, including harpin protein, thiamine, Cu, Zn, and salicylic acid [31, 33, 45, 109, 110].

NP-based nanoencapsulation (e.g., chitosan, alginate, dextran, cellulose, and starch) consistently improves the stability, controlled release, and bioefficacy of agrochemicals (insecticides, herbicides, fungicides, and fertilizers), while reducing toxicity and environmental losses. Overall, these biopolymeric nanocarriers represent a practical and sustainable nano-delivery platform for modern agriculture, although further field-scale validation and standard safety assessment are still needed.

sec.title: NPS-mediated plant defense priming and stress-tolerance mechanisms
sec.p: Plant defense is not limited to resistance against pathogens but includes interconnected structural, biochemical, transcriptional, and antioxidant responses to both biotic and abiotic stresses. NPSs, particularly CSNPs, contribute to these responses by acting as bioactive elicitors and as carriers of defense-promoting compounds [1, 2, 4, 5]. However, most mechanistic evidence currently concerns CSNPs, whereas the immune-modulating properties of nanocellulose, alginate, starch, pectin, and other NPSs remain insufficiently investigated.

The high surface area and positively charged amino groups of CSNPs promote their interaction with negatively charged plant cell walls and plasma membranes, facilitating the initiation of early defense signals [1, 4, 5]. These responses involve calcium-dependent signaling, transient ROS and nitric oxide production, and activation of defense-related genes. In pearl millet, highly acetylated CSNPs enhanced downy mildew resistance by promoting nitric oxide generation and earlier PR1 and PR5 expression [22]. CSNPs are therefore considered defense-priming agents that prepare plants to respond more rapidly and strongly to subsequent pathogen infection or environmental stress without maintaining defense continuously at its maximum level [1, 4, 5, 22, 44].

CSNP-induced priming activates key defense enzymes involved in phenylpropanoid metabolism, cell-wall reinforcement, and fungal cell-wall degradation (Fig. 2). In chickpea, thiamine-loaded CSNPs increased PPO, PO, β-1,3-glucanase, chitinase, chitosanase, and protease activities, thereby enhancing resistance to wilt disease [45]. CSNP treatment similarly induced PO, PAL, and chitinase in rice against Rhizoctonia solani [46], while foliar application to finger millet increased chitinase, β-1,3-glucanase, chitosanase, protease inhibitor, PO, and PPO activities [39]. In maize, Cu–CSNPs increased superoxide dismutase (SOD), PO, PPO, and PAL activities, including 1.5–2-fold higher POD and 2–3-fold higher PAL activities [32].

caption.p: Proposed integrated mechanism of NPS-mediated plant defense priming and stress tolerance. NPSs, particularly chitosan nanoparticles (CSNPs), can contribute to crop protection through two complementary routes. First, they may directly inhibit pathogens or serve as carriers for antimicrobial and defense-promoting compounds. Second, interactions of CSNPs with plant surfaces can initiate early signaling events involving controlled reactive oxygen species and nitric oxide production, followed by regulation of defense-related genes and transcription factors. Downstream responses include induction of PAL, PO/POD, PPO, chitinase, β-1,3-glucanase, SOD, and catalase; accumulation of PR proteins, phenolics, and flavonoids; and reinforcement of structural barriers. These interconnected responses enhance resistance against fungal, bacterial, and viral pathogens and improve tolerance to drought, salinity, heavy-metal toxicity, and oxidative stress. Solid arrows indicate mechanisms supported by the literature reviewed here, while any proposed receptor-level or intermediate signaling steps should be shown with dashed arrows where direct evidence for NPSs remains limited

sec.p: NPSs also function as carriers for compounds that reinforce plant defense. HarpinPss encapsulation in CSNPs improved its bioavailability and induced PO and PAL activities in tomato [109]. Similarly, CSNPs carrying thiamine [45], salicylic acid [110], essential oils [95], Cu, or Zn [32, 33] combine the intrinsic elicitor activity of chitosan with the biological activity of the loaded compound. At the molecular level, highly acetylated CSNPs increased PR1 and PR5 expression in pearl millet [22], while CSNP treatment altered genes related to PAL, PO, PPO, catalase, and SOD. In Nicotiana glutinosa, CSNPs inhibited alfalfa mosaic virus replication and stimulated innate immune responses [44]. In tomato, Thymus vulgaris essential-oil-loaded CSNPs upregulated WRKY transcription factors and defense-related genes while increasing phenolic and flavonoid contents and antioxidant enzyme activities against Fusarium solani [95]. Salicylic-acid-functionalized CSNPs also improved the delivery and biostimulatory activity of this endogenous defense signal [110].

ROS regulation links pathogen defense with abiotic stress tolerance. NPSs induce an early ROS signal followed by activation of antioxidant enzymes such as SOD, catalase, and POD to restore redox homeostasis. Enhanced antioxidant activity has been reported after Cu–CSNP treatment in maize [32], under water-limited conditions [40], and in CSNP-treated plants exposed to pathogen infection and heavy-metal stress [22, 34].

The protective effects of CSNPs consequently extend beyond pathogen resistance. Under drought, CSNPs improved wheat performance [26], while foliar treatment in maize increased biomass, root length, chlorophyll concentration, K⁺ uptake, soluble proteins, and antioxidant enzyme activities [28]. CSNPs combined with Myco-Root also improved photosynthesis, antioxidant activity, growth, and essential-oil production in water-stressed Lallemantia iberica [40]. Chitosan-based materials can additionally alleviate salinity-induced oxidative injury and physiological disturbances [2]. In Cd-stressed tomato, foliar-applied CSNPs increased shoot biomass, photosynthesis, and SPAD values while decreasing H₂O₂ and malondialdehyde accumulation, indicating improved ROS control and reduced membrane injury [34]. sec.p: Collectively, NPSs, especially CSNPs, activate interconnected defensive responses involving nitric oxide and ROS signaling, PR proteins, WRKY transcription factors, PAL, PO, PPO, chitinase, β-1,3-glucanase, antioxidant enzymes, phenolics, flavonoids, and structural reinforcement. These responses contribute not only to resistance against fungal, bacterial, and viral pathogens but also to tolerance against drought, salinity, heavy metals, and oxidative stress [2, 22, 28, 32, 34, 39, 44–46, 95, 109, 110]. However, future studies should distinguish the intrinsic effect of the NPS carrier from that of loaded metals, elicitors, or bioactive compounds and provide stronger mechanistic and field evidence for NPS classes other than CSNPs.

sec.title: Application of NPSs for encapsulation and nanocoating of agriculturally important microbial cells
sec.p: The efficacy of microbial inoculants in agriculture is constrained by complex soil environments and exposure to multiple biotic and abiotic stresses; consequently, NPSs have emerged as promising materials for encapsulation and nanocoating strategies aimed at improving microbial survival and functional performance [9, 10]. Conventional formulations often fail to protect microbial cells from desiccation, temperature fluctuations, oxidative stress, and antagonistic soil microbiota, resulting in reduced viability and inconsistent field outcomes [111]. In this context, NPSs such as CSNPs, AlgNPs, SNPs, and NC have attracted growing attention to form protective matrices or surface layers around living cells [10, 112]. The beneficial effects of NPS encapsulation arise from their ability to form hydrated, semipermeable polymeric matrices around microbial cells. These matrices reduce desiccation and oxidative damage, buffer rapid temperature and moisture fluctuations, and physically separate inoculants from antagonistic soil microorganisms while still permitting diffusion of water, oxygen, nutrients, and microbial metabolites. Gradual matrix swelling and biodegradation further enable controlled microbial release and sustained colonization of the rhizosphere. Importantly, NPSs matrices function not only as agrochemical carriers but also as delivery platforms for beneficial microbial inoculants, enabling synergistic biological effects in planta [8, 10, 11, 113, 114].

Encapsulation strategies physically entrap microbial cells within polymeric matrices, providing mechanical protection and controlled release. For example, Bacillus subtilis encapsulated in SNPs synthesized via ultrasonication formed spherical nanobeads (~ 245 nm) with a negative surface charge while retaining strong antifungal activity against Fusarium spp., Alternaria solani, and Botrytis cinerea, demonstrating that NPS encapsulation preserves microbial viability while enhancing functional efficacy [10]. Similarly, CNCs–based matrices, particularly CNCs–carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) nanocomposites, have proven highly effective for encapsulating the biocontrol fungus Trichoderma harzianum, forming porous Ca²⁺-crosslinked systems that maintain spore viability and promote fungal growth during storage [113]. More recently, a CNCs-reinforced CMC nanocomposite was shown to markedly enhance T. harzianum stability, osmotic stress tolerance, and sustained release within monoammonium-phosphate fertilizer granules, enabling efficient and durable microbial delivery in integrated fertilization systems [8]. In another example, chitosan–alginate nanocapsules crosslinked with humic acid enabled co-encapsulation of plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (Pseudomonas fluorescens) and NPK nutrients, achieving sustained nutrient release over 30 days and improved water retention, thereby supporting plant growth while reducing environmental nutrient losses [112].

Beyond encapsulation, NPSs also enable direct microbe–nanomaterial synergy under field conditions. For instance, T. harzianum combined with CSNPs enhanced nutrient uptake, antioxidant activity, plant growth, and garlic yield, demonstrating chitosan’s dual role as both nanocarrier and bioactive modulator [11]. In contrast, nanocoating approaches generate ultrathin protective layers directly on microbial cell surfaces without fully isolating cells from their environment, allowing continued metabolic activity and ecological interactions. Representative examples include layer-by-layer chitosan–phytate nano-armouring of B. subtilis strains BST8 and BST18, which significantly enhanced shelf life and biocontrol efficacy against sunflower leaf blight via seed priming [9], and metal–phenolic/alginate nanocoatings that improved foliar survival, nitrogen fixation efficiency, and rice growth while reducing chemical fertilizer inputs [115]. NC-based nanocoatings have also been used to regulate bacterial release from solid carriers, enabling diffusion-controlled release and prolonged microbial activity in soil systems [114]. Unlike encapsulation, nanocoatings preserve direct contact between microbial cells and the surrounding environment while improving surface adhesion, reducing mechanical damage, limiting desiccation, and enabling gradual release from seed or fertilizer surfaces.

Overall, NPS-based encapsulation and nanocoating complementarily enhance microbial survival and functionality in agriculture, positioning NPSs as key materials for next-generation bioformulations [9, 11, 111].

sec.title: Nanopriming of seeds with NPSs as an emerging trend in agriculture
sec.p: Nanopriming is a seed enhancement strategy in which seeds are treated with nanoscale materials to improve germination, seedling establishment, and stress tolerance. This approach regulates early physiological and biochemical processes, including redox balance and metabolic activation, and improves plant performance under abiotic stress [75, 116–118]. Compared with hydro-, osmo-, and hormone priming, nanopriming enables more effective nano–bio interactions at the seed surface. These interactions help suppress plant pathogens [76], and accelerate water uptake, control reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling [119].

NPSs are among the most promising materials for seed nanopriming [75, 116–118]. Commonly used NPSs include CSNPs, AlgNPs, NC and PNPs. Their unique physical and chemical properties help regulate hydration, redox balance, nutrient availability, and signaling during seed imbibition [118, 120]. During seed imbibition, NPSs form hydrated nanoscale interfaces that improve water uptake and uniform moisture distribution while facilitating controlled transport of nutrients and signaling molecules. Their high surface area promotes interaction with the seed coat, resulting in balanced ROS signaling, activation of hydrolytic enzymes, accelerated reserve mobilization, and earlier seedling establishment.

Many studies report clear benefits of NPS-based nanopriming across crop species. In lentil (Lens culinaris L.), priming with CSNPs at 200 ppm increased germination, root and shoot length, seedling biomass, and vigor indices compared with non-primed seeds [121]. These effects were linked to higher activities of amylase, protease, phytase, and dehydrogenase, indicating improved mobilization of seed reserves. Field experiments confirmed better emergence, higher yield components, and increased grain yield in CSNPs-primed lentil plants [121].

In cereals, nanopriming also improves seed performance [75, 116]. Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) seeds primed with CSNPs-AlgNPs showed higher germination percentage, germination energy, and germination index [116]. Priming increased sugars and proteins, reduced lipid peroxidation, enhanced antioxidant activity, and improved ROS control, leading to uniform and stress-resilient seedlings [116].

NPSs are also used in nano-enabled seed coatings. Alginate-based electrospun nanofiber coatings improved germination and seedling vigor of Astragalus membranaceus [122]. The coatings promoted defense enzyme activity and improved soil microbial composition, supporting early plant growth [122].

NC-based systems further extend the benefits of NPSs-mediated nanopriming. In rice (Oryza sativa L.), lignin-containing cellulose nanofiber hybrids enhanced germination and seedling growth under salt stress. These effects were associated with improved Na⁺/K⁺ balance and higher expression of salt-responsive genes, especially in salt-sensitive genotypes [117]. Once seeds are nanoprimed with NPSs, both germination and salt tolerance are improved through better seedling establishment and ion regulation [117]. Pectin nanospheres have also improved wheat seed germination and early growth, showing the wide applicability of nanopolysaccharide systems [75].

In general, NPSs-based nanopriming has been tested in legumes, cereals, and medicinal crops. Reported benefits include faster and more uniform germination, stronger seedlings, improved antioxidant capacity, better ion balance, and higher yields in field trials. These findings highlight NPSs-based nanopriming as a simple, eco-friendly, and scalable approach for sustainable and climate-resilient agriculture [119, 120]. Based on the comparative analysis presented throughout this review, Table 5 summarizes the key physicochemical requirements and evidence-based selection of NPS platforms for major agricultural applications.

sec.title: Future perspectives
sec.p: NPSs are promising candidates for mitigating abiotic and biotic stress factors in climate change–era agriculture. The major constraints limiting agricultural productivity include: (i) soil salinity; (ii) shortage of water resources; (iii) agrochemical-resistant plant pathogens; and (iv) intensive use of mineral fertilizers and other hazardous agrochemicals. In this context, NPSs can play an important role in the development and application of innovative agrobiotechnologies.

Other emerging applications of NPSs include their use as biodegradable composite mulching materials [123] and in hydroponic cropping systems for the controlled release of indole-3-acetic acid [124], development of sustainable nutrient substrates [125], and hydrogel-based soilless cultivation systems [126]. In particular, hyperbranched cellulose nanocrystals combined with polylactic acid (PLA) have been reported to form biodegradable mulching composites with promising agricultural potential [123].

It is also evident that under rapid and severe climate change, plants increasingly lose competitiveness against pathogens. Accordingly, eco-friendly nano-biocides such as NPSs are expected to be in high demand in agriculture. Several studies have already reported the use of NPSs against plant pathogens [17, 80, 81, 93].

Moreover, improving the efficiency of mineral fertilizers and reducing costs through NP-based loading or delivery systems has been demonstrated as a highly effective strategy [7, 59, 70, 127]. Despite some studies documenting the impact of certain NPSs on soil structure and properties [128], comprehensive investigations in this area are still lacking. Therefore, future research should evaluate the performance of NP-based systems under a broader range of soil conditions and irrigation scenarios, including their compatibility with different NPK fertilizer formulations. In our view, considering current agricultural demands, such technologies are among the most promising targets for commercialization.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: NPSs represent a versatile and sustainable class of nano-enabled materials for modern agriculture, combining biodegradability with multifunctional performance. The reviewed literature indicates that chitosan-, cellulose-, alginate-, starch-, pectin-, and dextran-based nanoformulations have demonstrated strong potential to improve nutrient-use efficiency under controlled experimental conditions via controlled/slow release of mineral fertilizers, while enhancing crop protection through nano-enabled loading and targeted delivery of agrochemicals, botanical actives, elicitors, micronutrients, and functional nano-additives. In addition, many NPSs, particularly CSNPs, exhibit intrinsic antimicrobial activity and can prime plant immunity by activating defense enzymes, antioxidant systems, PR proteins, and other defense-related genes.

Based on the evaluations summarized in the current review (Table 5), it was concluded that specific NP platforms are optimally suited for distinct agricultural purposes. Specifically, nanocellulose-based systems (CNF/CNC/BNC) represent the most suitable candidates for soil improvement, drought buffering, and slow/controlled fertilizer release, owing to their strong network-forming capability, high water-holding capacity, and diffusion-regulated nutrient release behavior. In contrast, nanoalginate formulations provide highly efficient encapsulation and delivery matrices for agrochemicals, micronutrients, and elicitors, due to ionotropic gelation and tunable release properties. Meanwhile, CSNPs emerges as the best-performing NPS for biological protection functions, demonstrating the strongest evidence for broad-spectrum antibacterial/antifungal activity, antiviral applications (including RNAi delivery), and enhancement of plant immunity through defense priming.

Future progress requires field-scale validation, standardized characterization and reporting practices, and rigorous assessment of environmental fate and biosafety, including impacts on soil microbiomes. Overall, NP-based nanoformulations offer a promising pathway toward efficient, low-residue, and climate-resilient crop production.
